meta.subject: the Texas–Mexico border as a policy issue — Operation Lone Star and state border spending, Eagle Pass and Shelby Park, the buoys and the wall, state versus federal authority, immigration enforcement, cross-border trade and the ports of entry, and the politics of the border counties
meta.subtitle: Oct 1 to Oct 17, 2026. Each dot is one post with 1K+ views about the Texas border and Eagle Pass, plus every post repeating an earlier one, in the lane for what it argues. Higher and bigger means more views. White means 90% or more the same words as an earlier post, with a white line back to it. Coloured lines link a post to the post it quoted or replied to. Updated daily.

lanes.label: Activist judges are blocking the wall
lanes.description: The Big Bend injunction is framed as lawless judicial obstruction of Trump's border wall, with judge Cardone and leftist groups accused of keeping the border open to invaders.

lanes.label: Big Bend wall halt is a victory
lanes.description: The ruling is celebrated as a win for landowners, river guides, conservationists and border-county locals who oppose the wall's cost, its environmental waivers and its seizure of land and park.

lanes.label: Abbott's border emergency and spending

lanes.label: Lone Star vindicated by $7.5B reimbursement
lanes.description: The $7.5 billion federal reimbursement is presented as proof that Texas was right to act when Biden failed, and Operation Lone Star as a model of state border security that is now paying off.

lanes.label: Eagle Pass as Biden-era invasion
lanes.description: Eagle Pass footage and crime stories are used to argue that Democrats opened the border, that migrants are criminals and cartels, and that voters must stay Republican to avoid a return.

lanes.label: Border counties and the Texas midterms
lanes.description: The border is treated as an electoral battleground, with border counties, the Rio Grande Valley and Hispanic voters as swing blocs in the Abbott–Hinojosa and Cruz–Talarico races and in the legislature.

lanes.label: Pushback

ALERT: 🚨  Federal court blocks Trump administration border wall in Texas’ Big Bend region. 

On Friday, October 2, 2026, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone of the Western District of Texas in El Paso granted a preliminary injunction in a case filed by the Center for Biological Diversity, Friends of the Ruidosa Church, and a local river guide and landowner. 

The order says the Department of Homeland Security, Secretary Markwayne Mullin, and Customs and Border Protection may not build border barriers or related infrastructure, or do construction or ground-disturbing work, in the Big Bend sector unless they comply with all applicable laws.

Cardone found the plaintiffs are likely to succeed on at least one claim, that they would face serious, irreparable harm without a pause, and that the balance of equities and the public interest favor the injunction. The order stays in place while the court decides the full case, which was filed in April.

The dispute centers on DHS waivers, issued under a 1996 border-infrastructure statute, that set aside a long list of environmental, historic-preservation, and park laws so work could move faster. 

Challengers say those waivers were used improperly inside and around Big Bend National Park and Big Bend Ranch State Park. Clearing near Santa Elena Canyon began in early August; after public and bipartisan criticism, CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott briefly paused work, and activity later resumed in parts of the region. 

Planned projects in the park have been described as roads, vehicle barriers, and surveillance rather than the taller steel walls used elsewhere.The Big Bend sector covers more than 500 miles of the Rio Grande frontier in remote West Texas. 

The work is part of a much larger southern-border infrastructure program. A separate suit tied to flooding concerns near Presidio had earlier failed to win an injunction after a related waiver was issued.

The administration has said it stands by its assessment and remains confident in its legal authority to secure the border while accounting for the region’s landscape. 

The injunction does not end the broader wall program; it blocks this sector’s construction unless the government follows the laws the waivers sought to suspend, pending a final ruling.

Sources: reporting from the Associated Press, Reuters, The New York Times, and the Center for Biological Diversity (October 2–3, 2026).

posts.name: Owen Gregorian
posts.text:
Federal Judge Pauses Trump's Border Infrastructure Project in Big Bend National Park | Randy Clark, Breitbart

United States District Judge Kathleen Cardone issued an emergency injunction blocking the Trump administration from continuing work to construct vehicle barriers, patrol roads, and accompanying lighting in the West Texas Big Bend Sector. The ruling, handed down in El Paso on Friday, also halts any construction or ground disturbance within Big Bend National Park in remote West Texas.

Cardone issued the order after considering witness testimony in a case brought against Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin by Friends of the Ruidosa Church et al. The case challenges the federal government’s use of waiver authority related to environmental law to speed completion of the project.

Laiken Jordahl, national public lands advocate for the Center for Biological Diversity, a plaintiff in the lawsuit, issued a statement on the injunction, saying, “This is a historic victory for Big Bend and everyone who loves this wild corner of Texas. No administration has the right to destroy a crown-jewel national park for political theatre. With a federal court ordering the bulldozers to stop, Big Bend gets to breathe. But this fight is far from over. We won’t rest until Big Bend’s environmental protections are fully restored and the illegal waiver that allowed so much destruction is gone for good.”

Another plaintiff in the lawsuit is a Big Bend river guide and landowner. The lawsuit challenges the federal government’s waiver process used to construct border security infrastructure within Big Bend National Park, Big Bend Ranch State Park, and throughout the Big Bend Region.

In her ruling, Judge Cardone wrote, “The Court finds that Plaintiffs are likely to succeed on the merits of at least one of the claims in suit, that there is a likelihood that they will suffer serious, irreparable harm without an injunction, and that the balance of the equities and the public interest weigh in their favor.”

Cardone’s instruction to the federal government included the following: “Effective immediately and until the Court orders otherwise, Defendants SHALL NOT build border barrier or related infrastructure, or engage in any construction or ground-disturbing activities, in the Big Bend Sector until and unless Defendants comply with all applicable laws.”

As Breitbart Texas reported, in mid-August, U.S. Customs and Border Protection Commissioner Rodney Scott paused the infrastructure projects underway within Big Bend National Park.

Politicians on both sides of the aisle had been closely scrutinizing the projects, Breitbart Texas reported. Senator John Cornyn (R-TX) joined local politicians and James Talarico, the Democratic nominee in Texas’s 2026 U.S. Senate race, in opposing the border security enhancements.

The installation of physical barriers within the state has also proven unpopular with ranchers outside the park. Many private landowners have met the projects with skepticism, and many hold large tracts of land and worry about losing access to parts of their property because of border barrier construction. Ranchers also worry that increased federal presence on their property will affect livestock and hunting.

CBP has clarified that its infrastructure plans within Big Bend National Park would involve only constructing one new access road, improving existing roads, installing detection technology, and placing vehicle barriers in limited, strategic locations.

According to CBP, the work would not include building a 30-foot border wall in the park.

President George W. Bush appointed Judge Cardone as a district judge in the Western District of Texas in 2003.

The case is styled “Friends of the Ruidosa Church et al. v. Mullin et al. (Case No. 3:26-cv-01099-KC)” in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Texas.

posts.text:
While Big Bend's border wall is tied up in a major legal fight right now, there's a bigger story hiding behind it: millions of acres of Texas public land.

The Texas General Land Office owns a massive checkerboard of parcels across the exact border counties, Hudspeth, Presidio, and Brewster, where the wall and vehicle barriers are planned. This isn't just any state land, it's Permanent School Fund (PSF) land, over 13 million acres constitutionally dedicated to funding Texas public schools.

It's leased out in scattered pieces, acre by acre, mostly to ranchers and oil and gas. Ranchers depend on it for water access. River guides depend on it for their livelihoods. Billy Miller, a river guide and landowner, testified at the October 2 hearing. Asked what Big Bend means to him, he said: "The wilderness of Big Bend saved my life."

So who's supposed to be protecting this land? Commissioner Dawn Buckingham runs the @TXGLO She spoke out once in July, after contractors cleared GLO land without permission. Since then, silence.

Turns out there's a reason. A reporter requested GLO's communications with the federal agency building the wall. GLO tried to keep it secret, but Texas law required them to show their own excuse to the reporter. It backfired: the letter admitted GLO's been in "regular contact" with CBP the whole time.

This isn't a neutral official caught in the middle. Buckingham publicly pledged to help Trump's deportation push by donating state land. Trump has endorsed her. She calls herself a "staunch defender of the Trump agenda." Her biggest donors are oil, gas, and ranching interests, the same industries leasing this land. Her July objection wasn't about protecting ranchers. It was lip service.

A wall that disrupts these leases doesn't just hurt ranchers, it threatens money meant for Texas kids. This administration has already cut Medicaid, SNAP, and school meal funding. Vanity projects over kids. That's the pattern.

The land, the water, the schools, all of it's on the table. I don't think many Texans voted for this.

#DemsUnited
